title: Strongly polynomial planar minimum-cost flow
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic strongly polynomial algorithm for minimum-cost flow in a planar directed graph whose worst-case number of arithmetic operations and comparisons is \(o(n^{2}\log(n+2))\), where \(n\) is the number of vertices? The algorithm must return an exact minimum-cost feasible flow, or correctly report infeasibility, for all rational capacities, costs and vertex supplies.
why: This asks how much planarity can accelerate exact flow optimization when numerical magnitudes cannot enter the operation count. It separates combinatorial graph structure from progress that relies on bounded capacities and costs.
status_note: The 2013 source states the strongly polynomial speedup as open. The model was recovered on 13 September 2026 and a bounded subsequent-work check found only a verified abstract for a different numeric regime, not a resolution of this target. Status is source_open; source proofs were not independently verified.

sentences: Minimum-cost flow assigns capacity-respecting arc flows that meet prescribed supplies and minimize total cost.
The question asks for an asymptotic improvement over the quadratic-times-logarithmic bound on planar graphs.
The algorithm must be strongly polynomial, so numerical magnitudes cannot enter its arithmetic-operation bound.
A later nearly linear algorithm for polynomially bounded integer data does not by itself meet that requirement.
A resolution would show whether planar structure yields a faster exact algorithm independently of the size of the input numbers.

definitions: The input is a finite directed graph with vertex set \([n]\), no loops and at most one arc for each ordered pair of vertices; opposite arcs are allowed. The underlying undirected graph is planar, and a combinatorial planar embedding is supplied. Thus the number of arcs is \(O(n)\). Each arc \(a\) has a finite rational capacity \(u_a\geq0\) and rational cost \(c_a\), and each vertex \(v\) has rational supply \(b_v\), with \(\sum_v b_v=0\). All numerators and positive denominators are encoded in binary; no magnitude bound is imposed. A feasible flow assigns rational \(f_a\) with \(0\leq f_a\leq u_a\) and \(\sum_{a\text{ out of }v} f_a-\sum_{a\text{ into }v}f_a=b_v\) at each vertex. Its cost is \(\sum_a c_a f_a\). Strong polynomiality means a bound polynomial in \(n\) on exact rational arithmetic operations, comparisons and index/memory operations, independent of all numeric bit lengths, together with a polynomial bound in total input bit length on every intermediate number’s encoding length. Arithmetic uses addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by nonzero values. The algorithm has finite uniform code and no advice, randomness or oracle. The little-o improvement means that there is a function \(T(n)\) bounding its operation count on every such \(n\)-vertex input with \(T(n)/(n^{2}\log(n+2))\to0\). The source’s instruction to beat the stated bound is interpreted as an asymptotic little-o improvement, not merely a smaller leading constant. The simple planar-network convention prevents arbitrarily many parallel arcs from hiding an unbounded input size in \(n\).

context_blocks.text: Erickson’s question in the 2013 seminar report explicitly asks for a strongly polynomial algorithm improving the quadratic-times-logarithmic bound. The supply-and-capacity formulation is stated there; all-zero supplies give its minimum-cost circulation special case.

A 2022 preprint gives a nearly linear algorithm for planar minimum-cost flow with polynomially bounded integer costs and capacities. Those numeric restrictions are material: this result does not by itself answer the strongly polynomial question for arbitrary rational input data.

answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm with the exact flow guarantee, little-o operation bound and polynomial intermediate bit lengths, or prove that no such deterministic strongly polynomial algorithm exists. A speedup for bounded numerical data, an approximation algorithm, or a lower leading constant at the same asymptotic order does not answer the stated question.
